Hatchlings of the Anatolian rock lizard emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs with a snout-vent length of approximately 2.5 centimeters [Lb = approximately 2.5 centimeters], a modest size that reflects the energetic constraints of embryonic development within a cleidoic egg. The incubation period required to reach this hatching stage is heavily dependent on thermal conditions, with embryos incubated at a constant temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C] completing development and pipping the eggshell after approximately 56 days [ab = approximately 56 days]. This incubation duration is typical for lacertid lizards of comparable egg size and underscores the pronounced role of temperature in determining developmental rates. Under cooler regimes, the period would likely be extended, while warmer but sub-lethal temperatures would accelerate embryo growth. The hatchlings themselves are lecithotrophic for a brief period, relying on residual yolk reserves before making the trophic switch to active feeding on small arthropods. Their initial body length imposes constraints on the size of prey they can subdue, and they grow rapidly during the first few weeks of exogenous feeding, gradually increasing in both stature and mass as they transition into the juvenile stage.

Adult female Anatolian rock lizards ultimately attain a maximum snout-vent length of 7.4 centimeters [Li = 7.4 centimeters], whereas adult males of this species reach a slightly larger ultimate snout-vent length of 7.6 centimeters [Li = 7.6 centimeters]. This subtle sexual size dimorphism, with males averaging approximately two percent longer bodies than females, is a common pattern among lacertids and is often linked to intrasexual competition for territories and mating opportunities. The ultimate wet body mass of an adult female, derived from allometric relationships observed in related lacertids such as Podarcis muralis, is estimated to be approximately 7.98 grams [Wwi = approximately 7.98 grams]. This asymptotic mass reflects the culmination of somatic growth following the juvenile and sub-adult phases, during which individuals allocate resources primarily to increases in body length and mass. The relatively modest adult size of Anatololacerta anatolica, compared to some larger-bodied congeneric species, likely influences its foraging ecology, predation risk, and the energetic costs associated with egg production and territorial defense.

Reproductive activity in female Anatolian rock lizards is characterized by a moderate fecundity and multiple nesting events within a single active season. Gravid females produce clutches that range from three to eight eggs per clutch [N_R_i = three to eight eggs per clutch], a clutch size typical of small-bodied lacertids and one that likely varies with female body condition and resource availability. Under favorable conditions, field observations suggest that individual females are capable of producing between three and four separate clutches per year [F_R_i = between three and four separate clutches per year]. When both variables are considered, the maximum reproductive rate under optimal thermal conditions approximates 0.038 eggs per day when averaged across the annual activity period maintained at a temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. The energetic demands of this reproductive output are substantial, requiring females to maintain high ingestion rates to cover the costs of vitellogenesis and eggshell formation, particularly during the extended breeding season typical of populations in lower-elevation habitats. Additional observations indicate that clutch size is positively correlated with maternal body size, as larger females tend to produce larger clutches, and that the timing of the first clutch is influenced by the onset of spring temperatures, with earlier emergences leading to a longer reproductive window.

In laboratory settings maintained at a constant temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], individuals require approximately three years from hatching [tR = approximately three years from hatching] to reach the age at first reproduction. This relatively delayed onset of breeding, when compared to some small-bodied Mediterranean lacertids that may reproduce in their second year, is likely a consequence of the cooler and more variable thermal environment experienced by populations occupying higher-elevation refugia in Anatolia. The total lifespan of the species under similar captive conditions has been documented to extend to approximately ten years [am = approximately ten years] at 22 °C [T = 22 °C], and this longevity is notable for a lizard of its body size, suggesting that adult mortality rates are relatively low in stable habitats, allowing for extended periods of reproductive contribution across multiple breeding seasons. Seasonal variations in temperature can further modulate these life-history traits, as individuals experiencing warmer microclimates may accelerate their developmental pace, potentially reaching maturity earlier than their counterparts in cooler refugia.

The combination of a three-year delay to first reproduction (3 years) [tR = 3 years] at 22 °C [T = 22 °C] and a maximum lifespan of ten years [am = ten years] at 22 °C [T = 22 °C] places Anatololacerta anatolica on the slower end of the life-history continuum for lacertids of its size, a strategy that likely buffers populations against unpredictable environmental perturbations. The age at hatching, confirmed at 56 days [ab = 56 days] at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], provides a developmental baseline that, when combined with the hatchling snout-vent length of 2.5 centimeters [Lb = 2.5 centimeters], allows for the projection of growth trajectories under varying thermal scenarios. The ultimate adult sizes, 7.4 centimeters [Li = 7.4 centimeters] for females and 7.6 centimeters [Li = 7.6 centimeters] for males, represent the ceiling of skeletal growth after which energy is directed primarily toward maintenance and reproduction, culminating in a terminal adult mass of roughly 7.98 grams [Wwi = roughly 7.98 grams].
